say.text: Welcome to your very first class! I'll assume you know nothing yet, and that's perfect. Nothing is graded today. Just listen, and say each word back to me. Tap Next whenever you're ready, and tap any word to hear it again.

Chinese isn't written with letters. It's written with characters, like these. Pinyin spells the sounds of Chinese with the letters you already know, so you can read how a word sounds. For example, hello is written with two characters, and in pinyin it's n i, h a o.

See the little marks above the vowels? They're tones. In Chinese, the pitch of your voice is part of the word. The same syllable, ma, means four different things depending on its tone. Let's hear each one.
Tone one is high and flat, like singing one long note. Mā means mom. Listen, then say it back.
Tone two rises, like asking 'what?' in surprise. Má means hemp. Listen, then say it back.
Tone three dips low, then comes up a little. Keep it low and relaxed. Mǎ means horse.
Tone four falls sharply, like a firm 'No!'. Mà means to scold.
Some syllables are light and short, with no tone mark. That's the neutral tone. In māma, mom, the second ma is light. Listen.

Each character is one syllable, and it usually has a meaning. Many characters are built from parts. The character for mom has two parts: woman on the left, and horse on the right. The horse part gives the sound, ma. So mom is the woman word that sounds like ma.
One more trick. When two third tones come together, the first one rises instead, like tone two. So nǐ hǎo is said ní hǎo. You don't have to think about it: just copy the recording.
Now your first greeting: nǐ hǎo, hello. Listen, and say it back to me. You just spoke Chinese!

intro.text: Welcome to the class for First words. I'll show you 23 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: Chinese has no words for "a" or "the", and nouns never change for plural: 苹果 is "apple", "an apple", "the apples".
Verbs don't change either: 我要 (I want), 你要 (you want), 他要 (he wants).

why.text: Chinese words never change their form, so there are no 'a', 'the' or plural endings. Context and number words do that job instead.

body.text: Put 的 after a person to show what belongs to them: 我的 (my), 你的 (your), 妈妈的 (mom's).
With family and home, 的 is often dropped: 我妈妈, 我家.

why.text: 的 links a describing word or an owner to a noun, like English 's or 'of'. With close people (我妈妈), it's often dropped because the link is obvious.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Family and home. I'll show you 18 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: A number can't go straight before a noun. A measure word goes in between: 一个姐姐 (one older sister), 三个苹果.
个 (ge) is the all-purpose one. Others depend on the thing: 本 for books, 只 for many animals, 杯 for cups. 一 changes tone before them: yí ge, yì běn.

why.text: Chinese counts things with a measure word between the number and the noun, the way English says 'a cup of tea'. 个 is the all-purpose one.

rules.title: 很 + adjective: no 是 needed

body.text: To describe something, put the adjective right after the subject, usually with 很: 我的房间很大 (my room is big).
Don't use 是 here. Said lightly, 很 is just the link ("is"); stress it to mean "very".

why.text: In Chinese an adjective works like a verb ('to be big'), so you don't need 是. 很 sits in front, and is often barely stronger than plain 'is'.

body.text: 了 at the end of a sentence says something has changed: 我饿了 (I'm hungry now), 吃饭了 (it's time to eat).
It's about a new state of things, not just the past.

why.text: 了 at the end of a sentence marks that something has changed, a new situation, like English 'now'.

rules.title: Culture: greetings in mainland China and Taiwan

body.text: Handshakes are light, and at formal events a small nod or bow is polite. Give and take business cards with both hands, and read the card before putting it away.
"吃了吗？" (have you eaten?) is a friendly hello, especially with older people. It isn't an invitation: just answer "吃了，你呢？".
In Taiwan you'll hear "早安" and a softer, very polite tone. People address others by surname and title: 王老师 (Teacher Wang), 李经理 (Manager Li).
Gestures: to call someone over, wave with your palm facing down. Numbers 6 to 10 have one-hand signs (6 is thumb and little finger). Don't point at people with one finger.

why.text: Greetings show respect for age and status, and the mainland and Taiwan have their own habits and expressions.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for I want, I have, I like. I'll show you 18 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: 想 + verb is "would like to, feel like": 我想玩. 要 is stronger, "want, going to": 我要回家.
To say no, put 不 before it: 我不想.

why.text: 想 is a softer 'would like to'; 要 is a firmer 'want' or 'going to'. Choosing one shows how strongly you mean it.

body.text: 有 (to have) is the one verb you can't negate with 不. Say 没有 instead: 我没有哥哥.
Every other verb takes 不 for "don't": 我不喜欢.

why.text: 有 is the verb for 'have', and its negative is always 没有, never 不有. That's just how 有 works.

body.text: To turn a statement into a yes-or-no question, add 吗 at the end: 你喜欢狗 → 你喜欢狗吗？
To answer, repeat the verb: 喜欢 (yes) or 不喜欢 (no). There's no single word for yes.

why.text: 吗 at the end turns a statement into a yes-or-no question without changing the word order, so it's an easy way to ask.

rules.title: 两 for "two" before a measure word

body.text: When you count things, "two" is 两, not 二: 两只猫 (two cats).
二 is for counting out loud and in bigger numbers (十二, twelve).

why.text: 二 is used for counting and in numbers, but before a measure word Chinese uses 两, the way English says 'a couple of'.

body.text: Chinese questions keep the order of the answer. Put the question word where the answer would go: 这是猫 → 这是什么？ 他是老师 → 他是谁？
Don't add 吗 to a question that already has a question word.

why.text: Chinese keeps the word order of the answer: the question word sits where the answer will go. That makes questions easy to build.

rules.title: 在 + place + 上 / 下 / 里

body.text: To say where something is: thing + 在 + place + position word. 书在桌子上 (the book is on the table).
The position word comes after the place: 上 on, 下 under, 里 in.

why.text: Chinese describes a location as 'at the table's top': 在 + the place + a position word like 上, 下 or 里.

body.text: Another way to ask yes or no: say the verb or adjective, then 不, then again. 远不远？ (is it far?), 好不好？
The 不 in the middle is said lightly.

why.text: Saying the verb and its negative together (是不是, 'is or isn't') asks a yes-or-no question by offering both choices.

body.text: 太 + adjective + 了 means "too …": 太贵了 (too expensive).
Adjective + 一点儿 means "a bit more …": 便宜一点儿 (a bit cheaper), 大一点儿的 (a bigger one).

why.text: 太…了 expresses 'too' or 'so much', often with feeling. 一点儿 softens: 'a little'. Together they cover strength of description.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for My day. I'll show you 18 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: When something happens goes before the action, right after the subject: 我七点起床 (I get up at seven).
How you go somewhere also goes first: 我坐地铁上班 (I take the subway to work).

why.text: In Chinese, time words come before the verb, setting the scene first, because the language goes from the bigger context to the action.

rules.title: 了 after a verb: it happened

body.text: 了 right after a verb marks a finished action: 我去了公园 (I went to the park), 我看了一部电影.
To say it didn't happen, use 没 and drop 了: 我没去.

why.text: 了 after the verb marks that an action is completed. Chinese doesn't change the verb for past time, so 了 does that work.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Culture: food & table manners. I'll show you 6 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

rules.title: Culture: eating together in China and Taiwan

body.text: Dishes are shared in the middle of the table. If serving chopsticks (公筷) are offered, use them to take food. Never stand chopsticks upright in rice: it looks like incense at a funeral.
The host usually orders and pays, and friends happily argue over who gets the bill. When toasting an older person or your boss, hold your glass a little lower than theirs.
Tipping isn't expected in mainland China or Taiwan. In Taiwan you'll often hear 结帐 (jiézhàng) for the bill, and night markets are the place for street food.

why.text: Meals are shared in China, so the dishes go in the middle and hosts often serve their guests.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Telling stories. I'll show you 18 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: 又 A 又 B describes two qualities at once: 他又高又瘦 (he's tall and thin).
长得 + description says what someone looks like: 她长得像她妈妈.

why.text: 又…又… joins two qualities so the listener hears both at once: 'both … and …'.

body.text: Put 的时候 after an action to say "when" or "while" it happens: 我做饭的时候 (while I was cooking).
已经…了 is "already": 他已经走了 (he's already left).

why.text: …的时候 attaches 'time when' to a whole action, so the whole phrase sets the time, before the main verb.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Messages and plans. I'll show you 18 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: Verb + 不了 says something can't happen: 我去不了 (I can't go). Verb + 得了 is the opposite: 去得了.
不好意思 is the soft way to apologize or turn something down.

why.text: Putting 不了 after a verb says the result can't be reached: you try, but it won't happen.

body.text: 如果 starts the condition and 就 introduces the result: 如果下雨，我们就待在家里.
…怎么样？ at the end makes a suggestion: "how about …?"

why.text: 如果…就… pairs the condition with its result, like English 'if … then …', and the pair makes the logic clear.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Culture: holidays & celebrations. I'll show you 6 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

rules.title: Culture: holidays in mainland China and Taiwan

body.text: Spring Festival (the lunar New Year) is the biggest holiday: families reunite, sometimes travelling across the country, and children and young people get money in red envelopes (红包). In the north, families make dumplings together.

At the Mid-Autumn Festival people eat mooncakes and look at the full moon; in Taiwan it's also a time for barbecues. At the Dragon Boat Festival (端午节) there are boat races and zongzi, sticky rice wrapped in leaves.
Gifts: avoid clocks, because 送钟 (giving a clock) sounds like 送终 (attending someone's death). Avoid sets of four too: 四 (sì) sounds like 死 (sǐ, death).

why.text: Holidays follow the lunar calendar, so their dates move each year and their customs come from long traditions.

rules.title: 得 (děi): "have to"

body.text: To say you have to do something, put 得 (děi) before the verb: 我得交房租了, 'I have to pay the rent'.
This 得 is read děi, not de. It's casual and common in speech.

table: I have to pay the rent.
You have to come a bit early.

why.text: Chinese puts helping verbs like 得, 要 and 想 straight before the action, so the order is: who, then 'have to', then the action.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Health and feelings. I'll show you 18 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: 从 + time + 开始 says when something started: 我从昨天开始发烧 (I've had a fever since yesterday).
Pain is just body part + 疼: 我头疼.

why.text: 从…开始 marks the starting point of something that continues, like English 'since' or 'starting from'.

body.text: 应该 is "should", 最好 is "you'd better", and 我建议你 is "I suggest you".
要是我是你 (if I were you) is followed by 我会… (I would …).

why.text: Chinese advice is often softened (最好, 应该, 不如) to stay polite, because direct orders can sound rude.

intro.text: Welcome to the class for Dating & relationships. I'll show you 12 new words and phrases, one at a time. Listen to each one, look at what it means, and say it out loud. Then we'll look at a rule that helps you use them. Nothing here is graded.

body.text: Many people meet through friends, classmates or work, and family-arranged introductions (相亲 xiāngqīn) are still common, especially in your late twenties.
Accepting a compliment by playing it down is polite: 哪里哪里 (oh, not at all) is the classic reply. Saying a flat "thank you" is fine too among young people.
Dating is often talked about with an eye on the future, so asking early what someone is looking for isn't unusual.

why.text: Dating in China often involves family expectations, so relationships can move toward meeting the family sooner.

body.text: Sweet, playful compliments go down well: 你笑起来好甜 (your smile is so sweet) or praise for someone's taste or voice.
Comments on someone's body are much more forward in Chinese than in English; stick to smiles, style and personality.
撩 (liáo) is the everyday word for flirting, and 有戏 (yǒuxì) means "there's a chance".

why.text: Modesty is valued in China, so people often turn down compliments politely instead of saying thank you.

body.text: Face (面子) matters: avoid correcting or criticizing someone in front of others, and leave them a polite way out.
A direct "no" is rare. "我考虑一下" (let me think about it) or "不太方便" (not very convenient) often mean no. When praised, play it down: "过奖了" or "哪里哪里".
Questions about your age, salary or whether you're married are ordinary small talk in China, not rude. The number 4 is unlucky and 8 is lucky, in mainland China and Taiwan alike.
Tones change meaning: 买 (mǎi) is buy and 卖 (mài) is sell; 汤 (tāng) is soup and 糖 (táng) is sugar.

why.text: Face (面子) is about respect and dignity, and wrong tones can change a word, so both modesty and careful pronunciation help.

rules.title: 说得对: how well something is done

body.text: Verb + 得 + description says how something is done: 你说得对 (you're right, lit. you said it right), 他跑得很快.

why.text: 得 after a verb links it to how well it's done, so the description comes after the action.

rules.title: 虽然…但是… and 一方面…另一方面…

body.text: 虽然 (although) is paired with 但是 (but) in the second half. Unlike English, Chinese uses both: 虽然很难，但是值得.
一方面…另一方面… balances two sides of an argument.

why.text: These pairs set up the sentence's logic in advance: 虽然…但是… prepares a contrast, 一方面…另一方面… weighs two sides.

body.text: 您 is the respectful "you" for older people, customers, bosses and strangers in formal settings. 你 is for everyone else.
People are often addressed by surname + title: 王总 (Director Wang), 李老师 (Teacher Li).

why.text: 您 is the polite 'you', shown to elders, teachers and customers. Respect for age and status is an important part of Chinese politeness.

body.text: 把 moves the object before the verb when you do something to it: 把盐递给我 (pass me the salt).
It's very common in requests and instructions.

why.text: 把 brings the object before the verb to focus on what you do to it and how it ends up.

已读不回 (read, no reply) is the Chinese "left on read". Saying 晚安 (good night) is a sweet way to end an evening chat.

body.text: 土味情话 (tǔwèi qínghuà, "country-flavored love lines") are deliberately corny pick-up lines, hugely popular online. Many are puns, like 缺点 (flaw) heard as 缺 + 点你 (missing a bit of you).
They're used as a joke you share, not a serious move. The best reply is a laugh and 好土啊 (so cheesy!).
Teasing is affectionate (服不服?, admit it!) but keep it light and mutual.

why.text: Cheesy lines (土味情话) are a playful game online, so they're said with a smile, not to be taken seriously.

rules.title: Culture: internet slang and Taiwan's style

body.text: Online slang spreads fast: 666 (from 溜, smooth) means you're skilled; 永远的神 ("eternal god", written YYDS) is the GOAT; 点赞 is to like a post; 躺平 (lying flat) is opting out of the rat race.
牛 means awesome: "太牛了" is fine anywhere, but avoid the longer, vulgar version you'll see online.
Taiwan uses 超 + adjective all the time (超好吃, super tasty), 讚 for great, and soft particles like 啦 and 喔. Northern mainland speech adds 儿 to many words. Taiwan writes traditional characters, like 讚.

why.text: Chinese internet slang grows fast online, and Taiwan has its own words and expressions.

rules.title: Chengyu: four characters, one story

body.text: Chengyu are idioms of four characters, most from old stories. 画蛇添足, 'draw a snake and add feet', means to ruin something by overdoing it.

why.text: Chengyu keep the compact style of classical Chinese, where each character carried a whole word, so four characters can tell a whole story.

rules.title: Telling a story: 原来, 结果, 好在

body.text: 原来 (yuánlái), 'it turns out', reveals the twist. 结果 (jiéguǒ), 'as a result', tells what happened next.
更糟糕的是, 'what's worse', adds the last straw, and 好在 (hǎozài), 'luckily', brings relief.

table: In the end, as a result…

why.text: Chinese verbs don't change for time, so these linking words do the work of showing how events follow each other.

body.text: Meeting the parents (见家长 jiàn jiāzhǎng) usually means the relationship is serious. Call them 叔叔 (uncle) and 阿姨 (auntie), and use 您.
Bring a gift: good fruit, tea, or a local specialty. Avoid clocks (送钟 sounds like attending a funeral) and anything in fours.
Praise the cooking and offer to help clear up; the parents may well insist you sit down.

why.text: Meeting the parents is a big step in China, and gifts and respect for elders show you take the relationship seriously.

body.text: Refusals are often indirect: 我最近有点忙 (I've been a bit busy lately) or 我们还是做朋友吧 (let's just be friends). Take them as a no, kindly.
Asking to add someone on WeChat is the normal way to ask for their contact. If they offer to add you instead, or change the subject, let it go.
A gracious exit like 是我误会了 (I misread things) or 跟你聊天很愉快 leaves a good impression.

why.text: Saying no directly can cause someone to lose face, so many people refuse politely and indirectly.
